concept.name: Statistical arbitrage
concept.definition: A family of quantitative, typically market-neutral strategies that exploit statistical mispricings among large portfolios of related securities, using short-horizon mean reversion and factor models rather than the strict riskless mispricing of classical arbitrage. Pairs trading is the canonical example; profits are expected values over many small trades, not risk-free arbitrage.
concept.intuition: Instead of one guaranteed mispricing, stat arb places hundreds of small, hedged bets that each have a slight statistical edge, so the law of large numbers does the work.
concept.mechanics: Models estimate expected short-horizon returns from residuals after removing factor exposures; portfolios are built long undervalued and short overvalued securities, neutralized to market and common factors, and turned over quickly. Gatev et al. (2006) link pairs-trading profits to temporary mispricing of close substitutes with a common return factor.
concept.failure_modes: Model risk and regime shifts: estimated relationships degrade exactly when correlations spike in crises, and deleveraging events (e.g., August 2007 quant unwind) cause many stat-arb books to lose simultaneously.
concept.misconceptions: That 'arbitrage' here means riskless profit; statistical arbitrage is a set of probabilistic bets that can and do produce extended losses.
concept.example: A fund residuals-neutralizes 2,000 U.S. stocks against sector and style factors, shorts stocks 2 sigma above their model price, buys those 2 sigma below, and rebalances daily.

citations.source: Gatev, Goetzmann, Rouwenhorst, Pairs Trading: Performance of a Relative Value Arbitrage Rule (SSRN)
